findings.issue: GetPropertyIdentifierLocation reads `property.ContainingType.DeclaringSyntaxReferences` instead of `property.DeclaringSyntaxReferences`. The syntax it gets is a type declaration, so the `as PropertyDeclarationSyntax` cast always yields null. The BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull diagnostic (used at line 985) therefore always has no location and is now silently dropped by the filter, including for source-declared properties. This is a regression of an existing diagnostic and contradicts C4, C5 and C10.

The wrapper drops every diagnostic whose location is not a syntax tree in the compilation, not just ones from metadata. Diagnostics for source types that already had a null or Location.None location are now lost, for example when GetIdentifierLocation returns null. This is broader than the stated scope. It can lose safety-relevant diagnostics and contradicts C4 and C5. A narrower fix would guard only the metadata-declared member cases.

`FirstOrDefault()?.GetSyntax().GetLocation()` now creates MemberNeedsKey with a null location for symbols that have no syntax. The new filter then discards it. The null-location case is only handled by the global filter, so any source-declared case with no syntax reference would also lose its diagnostic without a trace.

The text says diagnostics about members of such a type are reported by the defining assembly and must be fixed there. That over-claims. The defining project may not run the analyzer, and a NuGet package author may not have fixed anything. The change only suppresses these diagnostics in the consumer; it does not guarantee anyone reports them. The same wording appears in doc/analyzers/MsgPack004.md line 52.

The tests only cover the case where there are no diagnostics. They set SkipGeneratedSourcesCheck and have no regression test that BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull or MemberNeedsKey are still reported for source-declared types. That gap is why the broken GetPropertyIdentifierLocation went unnoticed.
